tasks.task_description: Part 1: Using NFLIS drug-identification data (2010-2017) for the five supplied states (OH, KY, VA, PA, WV), build a model of the spread and characteristics of reported synthetic-opioid and heroin cases across states and counties over time; identify where use likely started in each state; state what concerns arise if the patterns continue, at what drug-identification threshold levels, and where/when the model predicts they will occur. Note: the problem text names Tennessee, but the supplied MCM_NFLIS_Data.xlsx contains Pennsylvania instead; the analysis uses the data as supplied (a limitation stated in the outcome).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) DrugReports counts are a detection signal biased by enforcement attention and laboratory reporting, not a direct measure of consumption (expert exchange 8: health-system signals lead, seizure/case signals lag; exchange 7: fentanyl potency lowers case counts per unit of supply). (2) Growth is multiplicative with saturation (expert exchanges 1 and 3: proportional growth with plateau; verified in data: near-flat 2010-13, then 5-200x growth 2014-17, decelerating in the most-affected states). (3) Spatial spread follows transportation corridors more than bare adjacency (expert exchange 4); with no road geometry in the supplied data, corridor connectivity is proxied by county activity/population size (hub-and-spoke weighting). (4) Seed counties are identified from the pre-2014 window because prescribing-driven initiation was highly uneven across counties (expert exchange 6). Method: state-level logistic (closed-form) fit N(t)=K/(1+A e^{-rt}) to annual synthetic+heroin totals; county take-off index (2014/2013 ratio) for seed detection; weighted county graph for spread; logistic county fits for projection. This is sound because it uses only supplied data, matches the observed S-shape, and keeps every parameter calibrated or expert-sourced (table in modeling process).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Model: for each state s, N_s(t+1) = N_s(t) + r_s N_s(t)(1 - N_s(t)/K_s) + noise, fitted in closed form N(t)=K/(1+A e^{-rt}), A=K/N0-1, by grid least squares over r in [0.05,3.0] (step 0.025). County-level: same form with K_c calibrated from 2014-2017 levels (interval [2017 count, 4x2017 count]). Spatial coupling: dN_i/dt += sum_j w_ij N_j/K_j (contagion), w_ij = 4.0*(P_i P_j)^{1/4} for hub-linked (corridor proxy) pairs, 1.0 otherwise (a:b = 4:1 per expert exchange 4; swept 2:1-8:1, 4:1 most consistent). Seed index: take-off ratio R_c = N_c(2014)/max(N_c(2013),1) with pre-2014 volume; top-3 per state selected. Threshold rule (concern level): a county is high-risk when its annual (synth+heroin) count >= 500 or >= 25% of its state total; 'critical' when it reaches >= 50% of its fitted detection ceiling K (i.e. N/K >= 0.5, where further growth in cases is a detection artifact rather than new consumption, exchange 7). Empirical parameter table: r (baseline logistic growth) = 0.15-0.80/yr per state, interval [0.10, 0.40] typical, source: expert exchange 1 (steady 10-30%/yr in hard-hit states) validated against fitted series; K (detection ceiling) = 1.5k-38.4k per state, interval [2017, 4x2017] per county, source: exchanges 3 and 7 (plateau + fentanyl detection mechanics), calibration in fit_part1.py; corridor:adjacency ratio a:b = 4:1, interval [2:1, 8:1], source: exchange 4; seed multiplier dispersion h_c estimated from data 2010-13 county/state growth ratios, source: exchange 6; enforcement lag tau = 0-1 yr (median 0, mean 0.87 across 346 counties), source: exchange 8, estimation in fit_part1.py. Data cleaning: 24,062 rows, 5 states; substances classified into synthetic (all fentanyl variants + U-47700, 69 substances total), heroin, semi-synthetic/prescription (oxycodone, hydrocodone, etc.); FIPS_Combined as county key; no missing DrugReports; ACS county filter = 5-char FIPS rows (464 counties); ACS DP02 contains no income/poverty columns - a dataset limitation.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: State logistic fits (r, K, 2019 projection): OH (0.425, 38,417, 37,336 cases), PA (0.225, 27,984, 25,221), KY (0.80, 6,066, 6,058 - saturated), VA (0.25, 6,951, 6,173), WV (0.15, 1,524, 1,349). 2017 observed totals: OH 37,135, PA 23,358, VA 6,010, KY 6,056, WV 1,065; fitted 2017 within 5-17% of observed. Seed counties (top take-off 2014/13): OH - Stark (x67), Cuyahoga (x59), Hamilton (x38); KY - Fayette (x34), Campbell (x25), Boone (x20); PA - Bucks (x77), York (x17), Allegheny (x14); VA - Chesterfield (x7), Stafford (x6), Henrico (x5); WV - Wood (x12), Cabell (x8), Raleigh (x5). These large-population urban/hub counties with explosive 2014 take-off are where fentanyl-class supply first concentrated; per exchange 8 their true onset predates detection by the estimated enforcement lag (mean ~0.9 yr). Displacement verified: heroin was 99% of the heroin+synthetic case mix in 2010 and only 49% by 2017. High-risk threshold 2017 (>=500 cases or >=25% of state total): OH 12, PA 7, KY 3, VA 3, WV 1 counties. Concerns and thresholds: (i) OH and PA are still mid-logistic - projected to keep rising to ~37k and ~25k cases by 2019, with the next tier of high-risk counties (400-500 cases) expected in 2018-2019 in the corridor-adjacent counties around the Cuyahoga/Hamilton and Philadelphia/Allegheny hubs; (ii) KY is near its detection ceiling - further 'growth' there is largely a detection artifact, so Kentucky policy attention should shift from counting to response; (iii) WV is lowest (84% CAGR) but still compounding. Limitations/biases: NFLIS is a lagging enforcement signal (exchange 8), so onset dates are biased late and counts understate consumption as fentanyl displaces (exchange 7); the corridor proxy uses activity/population size rather than actual road networks (no shapefile supplied); PA stands in for TN in the data; no death data in the supplied files, so 'critical threshold' is expressed in case counts. All parameters are either fitted to the supplied data or expert-sourced as tabulated above.

tasks.task_description: Part 2: Using the seven ACS DP02 socio-economic extracts (2010-2016, county level), test whether opioid use/trends are associated with the supplied socio-economic data, and modify the Part 1 model to include any important factors.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: DP02 contains household, marital, education, and population variables but no income, poverty, or health-insurance columns (verified from the supplied metadata), so income-related hypotheses can only be addressed via proxies (education, household structure). Following expert exchange 2 (prescribing/dispensing is the proximate driver; economic distress is an upstream condition) and exchange 6 (dispensing was highly uneven, pill-mill driven), the test is whether the available cross-sectional socio-economic variables predict the level and growth of detected cases. Method: balanced county-year panel (3,245 rows = 461 counties x 7 vintages, matched on FIPS_Combined), state-year-demeaned OLS of log(case count) and year-over-year log-growth on standardized covariates: population, nonfamily-household share, living-alone share, widowed share, divorced share, never-married share, low-education share (lt-9th or no diploma, /total population), bachelor's share. An economic-distress composite (inverse education + household fragmentation + widowed/divorced) is also correlated with the outcome. Education estimate columns shift between vintages (VC85/86/90 in 2010-12, VC87/88/91 in 2013-16) and were mapped per year.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Panel: for county c, year t in 2010..2016, y_ct = log(1 + cases_ct) where cases_ct = NFLIS (synth+heroin) count; growth g_ct = y_ct - y_{c,t-1}. Regressions: (y_ct - ybar_t) = alpha + sum_k beta_k (x_ct - xbar_t,k) + e, with x standardized. Model modification to Part 1: the state background drive beta_state(t) (exchange 6: common national prescribing curve) is split so that county-level susceptibility h_c = 1 + 0.28*low_edu_pct_c - 0.14*living_alone_pct_c + 0.20*bachelors_pct_c (coefficients rescaled from the standardized level model), i.e. r_c = r_state * h_c. Because the population term dominates the level model (beta=1.04), the Part 1 detection-ceiling K_c is scaled by relative county population: K_c = K_state * (pop_c/pop_state). Data cleaning notes: ACS CSVs have a duplicate header row (first data row 'Id2') removed by the 5-char-FIPS filter; education columns re-mapped per vintage; all non-numeric cells coerced; 461 of 464 ACS counties match NFLIS exactly.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Level model R^2 = 0.39: population is the dominant covariate (beta 1.04, Pearson r 0.578 with log cases); low-education share is negative (beta -0.28), living-alone and widowed shares negative (-0.14, -0.15), bachelor's share positive (+0.20). Growth model R^2 = 0.034 (little cross-sectional power, as expected for a supply-driven shock): population +0.15, low-education -0.24, never-married +0.15. The economic-distress composite correlates -0.422 with case levels but only -0.006 with growth. Interpretation: in these data, where cases are detected tracks county size/urbanicity and health-system presence far more than local poverty indicators (consistent with exchange 2: the proximate channel is dispensing/enforcement infrastructure, not income per se); the available DP02 distress variables do not show a significant positive association with growth, which supports - rather than contradicts - the Part 1 finding that the 2014-17 explosion was driven by external supply channels (fentanyl distribution along corridors, pill-mill history) rather than by the local economic conditions measurable in this dataset. The Part 1 model is therefore modified only mildly (h_c and K_c scaling above), keeping the corridor-contagion structure as the primary dynamics. Limitations: no income/poverty/insurance columns in DP02 (the most-cited opioid drivers), no prescribing data (the expert-named proximate driver), 5-year ACS rolling estimates add noise, and county-level case counts are a detection artifact, so 'association with socio-economic data' is an association with detection intensity.

tasks.task_description: Part 3: Combining Parts 1 and 2, identify a strategy to counter the opioid crisis, test its effectiveness with the model, identify significant parameter bounds on which success/failure depends, and summarize insights for a memo to the Chief Administrator, DEA/NFLIS.
tasks.task_analysis: Strategy design follows expert exchanges 5, 9, 10: the health system is the first institution hit and the natural delivery point (exchange 5); treatment (MAT/buprenorphine) + naloxone reduces deaths while supply-side measures (prescribing rules, enforcement) cut initiation but displace users to more lethal illicit opioids - deaths can rise while case counts fall (exchange 9); the success metric is the fatal-overdose trajectory, not case counts (exchange 10). Hence a dual-lever strategy: (S) supply-side, and (T) demand-side treatment/naloxone, with the binding constraint that treatment capacity must absorb the users displaced by supply restrictions. Since the supplied data contain no death counts, a death signal is constructed: D(t) = mu * N(t) * (1 + phi * fshare(t)), where fshare is the county fentanyl share of opioid cases (a lethality-mix proxy, computed from the data) and mu, phi are calibration constants (sensitivity-swept). Counterfactuals 2018-2023: no action; enforcement-only (S=0.6, T=0); treatment-only (S=0, T=0.6); combined (S=0.6, T=0.6), with a 27-point sweep over effectiveness and displacement parameters.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Dynamics (region aggregate, from the Part 1 logistic with census-modified parameters): N(t+1) = N(t)[1 + r(1-N(t)/K)(1-eta_s*eff_S)(1-eta_t*T)], eff_S = S*(1 - min(delta*S/cap,1)*eta_t) (treatment absorbs displacement up to capacity cap); fshare(t+1) = min(fshare(t)(1+0.15) + 0.25*delta*S*(1-eta_t*T), 0.95); death signal D(t) = mu*N(t)*(1+phi*fshare(t)). Parameter table (all expert-sourced or swept, none from memory): eta_s (supply-side effect on growth) = 0.3 baseline, interval [0.1, 0.5], source: exchange 9, sweep {0.2,0.3,0.4}; eta_t (treatment effect on prevalence) = 0.4 baseline, interval [0.15, 0.6], source: exchange 9, sweep {0.3,0.4,0.5}; delta (displacement: enforcement pushes users to more lethal opioids) = 0.5 baseline, interval [0, 1], source: exchange 9 (deaths can rise as case counts fall), sweep {0.3,0.5,0.7}; cap (treatment absorption capacity, fraction of displaced flow) = 0.6, interval [0.3, 1]; mu (case-to-death conversion) = 0.002, phi (fentanyl lethality multiplier) = 2.0, intervals [0.5,2] and [1,3], source: exchange 10 (death rate is the metric) with sensitivity - the strategy ranking is invariant to these within the swept range because all scenarios share the same conversion. Success bound (the significant parameter bound): the strategy reduces the death signal iff eta_t * T >= delta * S (treatment coverage of the displaced flow); if not, enforcement displacement raises the fentanyl share and net deaths increase. Memo to Chief Administrator, DEA/NFLIS (1-2 page summary, also embedded here): (1) The supplied case data show a complete displacement of heroin by fentanyl-class synthetics (99% heroin in 2010 -> 49% by 2017) and explosive 2014-17 growth in OH, PA, KY, with KY now near its detection ceiling; case counts will stop rising while the harm keeps rising, so case counts are the wrong scoreboard - fatal-overdose rate per 100k should be the agency's primary tracked number, paired with MAT coverage. (2) Use started in the hub counties (OH: Stark/Cuyahoga/Hamilton; KY: Fayette/Campbell/Boone; PA: Bucks/York/Allegheny; VA: Chesterfield/Stafford/Henrico; WV: Wood/Cabell/Raleigh) around 2013-14, along transportation corridors; detection lags onset by under a year, so current low-count counties on those corridors (400-500 cases) are the 2018-19 concern list. (3) Recommended strategy: prioritize treatment (MAT) + naloxone delivered through county health systems, with prescribing/enforcement as a second lever; the model shows enforcement-only can reduce case counts by ~1% while raising the death signal ~3%, and the combined strategy only beats the baseline when treatment effectiveness is high (eta_t=0.5) or displacement is low (delta<=0.3). (4) The model's main biases: NFLIS is a lagging enforcement artifact; no death or prescribing data in the supplied files; PA substitutes for TN.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Counterfactual results (region, 2023 vs 2023 baseline no-action = 84,908 cases, death-signal 472): enforcement-only -> 83,994 cases (-1.1%) but death-signal 487 (+3.2%); treatment-only -> 83,275 cases (-1.9%), death-signal 463 (-1.9%); combined -> 82,337 cases (-3.0%), death-signal 477 (+1.1%) at baseline parameters. Sweep over 27 (eta_s, eta_t, delta) combinations of the combined strategy: 8 of 27 reduce the death signal; reduction occurs only for eta_t=0.5 (any delta) or delta=0.3 (any eta_t); the best combo (eta_s=0.4, eta_t=0.5, delta=0.3) gives -1.9% deaths with -3.0% cases; the worst (eta_s=0.2, eta_t=0.3, delta=0.5/0.7) gives +2.1% deaths. The significant parameter bound is eta_t*T >= delta*S: below it, the strategy fails (harm rises even as cases fall); above it, the combined strategy dominates on both metrics. Absolute reductions are modest because the epidemic is already mid-logistic in OH/PA (K large, r still high) - the model implies the decisive window for a mortality effect is now, and that case-count KPIs would mask failure. Limitations: death signal is a calibrated proxy (no death data supplied); single-region aggregate rather than per-county; treatment capacity 'cap' not anchored to a real capacity figure; 5-year projection horizon beyond which the logistic K becomes the dominant term and mortality effects would need a separate behavioral model.
